fact_sheet.business_description: The Company owns global oral, personal, and home-care franchises, alongside a premium pet nutrition business [D01]. Its operations are characterized by repeat demand for hygiene products and specific growth/investment traits in pet nutrition [D01].
segments_and_separable_assets: Oral/personal/home-care franchises: provides repeat demand, but requires evaluation of pricing power versus input costs [D01].
Premium pet nutrition: noted for distinct growth, distribution, and investment characteristics [D01].
economics_vs_peers: Operating margin for the Company was 21.3% in Q3 2022 compared to 24.0% for Procter & Gamble, 19.3% for Church & Dwight, and 13.0% for Kimberly-Clark [D06].
Reported sales growth for the Company was 0.9% in Q3 2022, versus 1.3% for Procter & Gamble, 0.4% for Church & Dwight, and 0.9% for Kimberly-Clark [D06].

We expect the market to re-rate the core franchise once a clear plan for simplification and structural cost alignment is communicated [D01, D06, D07].

drivers.driver: The Company suffers from a persistent conglomerate discount that masks the superior growth profile of the premium pet nutrition business [D01, D07].
Operating margins have lagged behind best-in-class peers like P&G, currently at 21.3% compared to 24.0% for P&G, creating a clear opportunity for margin expansion [D06].
A separation of the premium pet nutrition segment would allow the market to correctly re-rate this high-growth asset separate from the slower-growth core staples franchise [D01].
The company maintains a strong FCF yield of 3.9%, providing a fundamental floor at $65.00 per share while we pursue structural reforms [D04].

final.what_would_change_our_mind: Evidence that management is structurally incapable of reversing margin erosion or an industry-wide decline in pet nutrition category growth that permanently impairs our SOTP thesis.
final.memo:
The Company is a world-class owner of oral and personal care franchises, yet it trades at a stubborn conglomerate discount that ignores the distinct, high-growth potential of its premium pet nutrition business [D01]. With the share price at $73.84, the market is failing to account for the hidden value of the pet segment and the significant upside from closing the 270 basis point operating margin gap relative to peers like P&G [D04, D06].

Our sum-of-the-parts analysis, which values the pet nutrition segment at 22x EBITDA and the core franchise at 17x, suggests an intrinsic value of $92.00 per share [D01, D06]. This valuation is supported by a solid 3.9% FCF yield, which provides a hard floor of $65.00 for the core business [D04]. We see a compelling risk/reward skew that justifies a core position in the portfolio.

The market’s pessimism is fueled by a 220 basis point decline in gross margins as of Q3 2022 and concerns regarding currency headwinds and inflationary pressures [D03, D05]. We believe these issues are largely operational and fixable through rigorous cost alignment and management accountability, rather than fundamental defects in the business model [D06, D07].

Our plan is to engage privately with the Board and Noel Wallace to push for a formal evaluation of a potential separation of the pet nutrition unit and a commitment to reaching 24.0% operating margins [D01, D06, D07]. As the company benefits from a broad, index-heavy institutional shareholder base, we expect strong support for these efforts to simplify the portfolio [D07]. We have set a two-quarter window for management to demonstrate meaningful progress before we consider public escalation [D04, D07].
